newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major calls on Thatcher for inspiration.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major calls on Thatcher for inspiration.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major turned to his powerful predecessor Margaret Thatcher on Sunday for help in winning re-election but polls showed his party headed for thundering defeat on May 1.
Hoping to close the double-digit gap, Major derided Labour as copy-cat Conservatives without convictions and summoned "Iron Lady" Thatcher to rally the troops at Central Office.

Thatcher -- who has often damned her chosen successor with faint praise -- delivered a gung-ho message when she addressed 300 candidates and members of parliament, applauding Major's "magnificent stewardship of the last six years".
"It is thanks to him and the Conservative government that we have such a high level of prosperity and a high reputation in the world. I am here to support him," she said.
The woman who transformed Britain in the 1980s said the nation's current prosperity was no fluke.

"We Conservatives made it happen. The Conservatives have convictions, fundamental beliefs to serve the people and to create a framework of law within which enterprise and responsibility can flourish," she said to thundering applause.

Her visit hoped to dispel speculation she would be happy with a government run by new-look Labour: a message she underlined by saying Britain under any Labour government would see power shift to the trade unions and bureaucrats in Brussels.

Pouring scorn on the "conversion of convenience" that has shifted the once leftist Labour party to centre ground, the darling of the far right said: "Whatever the soft words, Labour is still interventionist in its very psyche."
Yet the fighting message sounds different on Thatcher's lips than on Major's and the Conservatives are struggling to win the upper hand against Labour in the countdown to polling day.

As the longest-serving British premier this century, Thatcher won plaudits for her tough style and was dubbed "the only man in the cabinet" during the tumultuous 1980s. Although her domination over her cabinet colleagues was ultimately the cause of her downfall the memory of it highlights the weak reputation that dogs her successor.
Major opted to talk tough on Sunday, saying the long election campaign was finally showing his opponents' true colours, blunders and outright lies.
New Labour might sound increasingly like the Conservatives but Major told BBC television: "The belief that they could deliver Tory (Conservative) policies is just idiocy."
"There's a difference between rhetoric and reality."
On taxes, European policy and a host of other key issues, the two parties were like "chalk and cheese".
He said Labour leader Tony Blair could not be trusted since he broke his word daily on everything from devolution to tax.
While attacking Blair time and again, Major also admitted making mistakes during his time in office and said he could not promise a gaffe-free rule.
"Of course we have made mistakes, I concede that," he said in a rare show of candour that mirrors Blair's own admission that the Conservatives got much right in their 18-year rule.
"I can't promise we won't make mistakes in the next government," he said.
Yet few except the die-hard expect Major to form another government.
According to an ICM poll for the Observer newspaper, Labour is on 50 percent against 30 percent for the Conservatives and 14 percent for the minority centrist Liberal Democrats.
An NOP poll for the Sunday Times gave Labour 52 percent, with the Conservatives on 28 percent. A MORI poll for the Sunday Mirror gave Labour 55 percent, the Conservatives 30 percent.
